seoDescription: Learn how to establish a baseline evaluation for your LLM application using LlamaIndex's powerful evaluation tools. This tutorial, part of the Bottoms-Up Development series, demonstrates how to assess the performance of a query engine built on your own data. Discover methods for measuring both hallucination and answer quality by using GPT-4 to generate a question dataset and evaluate responses. We cover setting up response and query evaluators to identify weaknesses and guide future improvements in your RAG pipeline.

chapters.title: Introduction to LLM Application Evaluation
chapters.description: This chapter introduces the importance of evaluating a query engine and outlines the challenges and LlamaIndex's two primary evaluation methods.

chapters.title: Notebook Overview and Initial Setup
chapters.description: A walkthrough of the evaluation notebook, covering the two evaluator types, API key setup, and loading documents while excluding specific metadata.

chapters.title: Building a Sub-Question Query Engine
chapters.description: This section covers the process of creating and configuring a sub-question query engine using multiple indexes and query engine tools.

chapters.title: Initial Test of the Query Engine
chapters.description: A quick test is performed with a simple question to confirm that the newly created sub-question query engine is working as expected.

chapters.title: Generating an Evaluation Question Dataset
chapters.description: This chapter details how to use LlamaIndex's DataSetGenerator with GPT-4 to automatically create a set of evaluation questions from the documentation.

chapters.title: Reviewing the Generated Questions
chapters.description: A random sample of the GPT-4 generated questions is reviewed to confirm their quality and relevance to the documentation.

chapters.title: Evaluating Response Hallucination
chapters.description: The first evaluation pass is executed using a ResponseEvaluator and GPT-4 to determine how many query responses are hallucinated.

chapters.title: Analyzing Hallucination Failures
chapters.description: This chapter investigates why certain responses were flagged as hallucinations by examining specific failed questions and their outputs.

chapters.title: Evaluating Answer Quality
chapters.description: The second evaluation pass is performed using a QueryResponseEvaluator to assess whether the responses and sources adequately answer the original query.

chapters.title: Analyzing Answer Quality Failures
chapters.description: An investigation into why certain answers were flagged for low quality, revealing issues like incomplete answers and potential false negatives from the evaluator.

chapters.title: Conclusion and Next Steps
chapters.description: The video concludes by summarizing the establishment of a baseline evaluation pipeline and highlighting its importance for guiding future improvements.

summary:
## The Challenge of LLM Evaluation

Evaluating a production LLM application is difficult due to several factors:
- **Unpredictable I/O**: Inputs can be anything, and outputs are non-deterministic.
- **Runtime**: Evaluations often require many expensive and slow LLM calls.
- **Cost**: API calls and resource usage can be significant.

## LlamaIndex's Core Evaluation Strategy

LlamaIndex provides a baseline evaluation framework that focuses on two key dimensions, using an LLM (like **GPT-4**) as the judge.

1.  **Faithfulness (Hallucination)**: Assesses if the generated **response** is factually grounded in the retrieved **source documents**. This is measured by the `ResponseEvaluator`.
2.  **Relevance (Answer Quality)**: Assesses if the **response** and its **sources** collectively provide a complete and correct answer to the original **query**. This is measured by the `QueryResponseEvaluator`.

## Setting Up a Baseline Evaluation

The video demonstrates a complete workflow for establishing an evaluation baseline.

1.  **Build a Query Engine**: A `SubQuestionQueryEngine` was created over multiple indexes, with each index represented as a tool with a description.
2.  **Generate an Evaluation Dataset**: Instead of writing questions manually, the `DataSetGenerator` was used with GPT-4 to automatically create a list of relevant questions based on the source documents.

> [!TIP]
> You can customize the prompts used by the `DataSetGenerator` to create higher-quality questions that are tailored to your specific use case, such as emulating an evaluator for a search pipeline.

## The Evaluation Workflow in Action

The evaluation process involves running the generated questions through the query engine and then passing the results to the evaluators.

- **1. Hallucination Check (`ResponseEvaluator`)**
    - **Process**: Compares the generated response against its retrieved source context.
    - **Example Result**: The pipeline found that **29 out of 40** responses were not hallucinated.

- **2. Answer Quality Check (`QueryResponseEvaluator`)**
    - **Process**: Compares the original query against the response and its sources.
    - **Example Result**: The pipeline found that only **19 out of 40** questions were answered satisfactorily.

## Analyzing Failures to Guide Improvement

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The numerical scores from evaluation are just a starting point. The real value comes from manually inspecting the failures to understand the root cause and guide improvements.

Analysis of the failed questions in the video revealed several types of problems:

- **Genuine Hallucinations**: The LLM invented an incorrect description for the `RouterQueryEngine`.
- **Failure to Retrieve**: The system couldn't find the correct information for a term like `GuidancePydanticProgram`.
- **Incomplete Answers**: The response about the `ReactAgent` was technically correct but unhelpful because it lacked a code example.
- **Inefficient Routing**: The `SubQuestionQueryEngine` asked the same question to multiple sub-indexes, indicating that the tool descriptions could be improved.
- **False Negatives**: The evaluator (GPT-4) sometimes incorrectly flagged a good answer as bad, highlighting that the evaluation process itself isn't perfect.
transcription:
## Introduction to LLM Application Evaluation

Hey everyone, Logan here from Llama Index, back with the next video in our Bottoms-Up development series. So far we've covered customizing your LLM and loading in documents, and now we're at a good point where we can actually assemble a query engine very easily.

But in order to make improvements further down the line, we actually need to evaluate how that query engine is performing. So in this video, we're going to kind of cover how to set up a baseline evaluation for your query engine.

Now, evaluating an LLM application in general is pretty hard. You could have any kind of input, you can't really control what the output is going to be—it could be anything. Runtime is a problem because we have to make many LLM calls, and also API costs, in terms of actual money and just resource usage depending on what LLMs or embeddings you're using. And so while solutions to these are still kind of in development, LlamaIndex does provide some basic evaluation pipelines with more planned in the future.

So right now when you set up a query engine in Llama Index, obviously you have your query engine, you send your query to it, and then on the output you get your response and sources. Using all three of these, we can actually evaluate how good that response was. And there's kind of two main ways of doing this right now.

First thing is you need a data set of questions to evaluate on. You could write this yourself or you could use our dataset generator to generate a data set of questions. Then using your questions that you have, you can evaluate both did the response hallucinate, and then also did the response and the sources actually answer the query.

So by looking at the response and the sources, we can kind of get a measure of hallucination. LLMs may make up information even when you're giving them the correct information. So we could kind of evaluate whether the response matches the sources by asking an LLM, a smarter LLM.

And same thing with the query, we can show another LLM that response and the query and basically figure out if that response actually answered that query.

## Notebook Overview and Initial Setup

And that's pretty much it. I've got a notebook here set up to guide us through this. Let's check it out.

So we've got our notebook here for our evaluation baseline. As I've noted in the top here, we have two types of evaluators. We have a response-source evaluator for measuring hallucination and our query-response evaluator for evaluating if the response actually answered the query.

Setting up is pretty simple. We just set up our API key. I'm going to append to my path so I can use the document loader that I created in the previous video. We can set up our kind of function here to help us load documents. You'll notice here that I'm excluding certain keys from the LLM in the metadata. So for all these keys, I only want them to be used for embeddings or for retrieval, but when the LLM actually reads the text, it's going to ignore these. Again, I covered that in the previous video.

I'm going to set that up. I'm going to load all our documents from the Llama Index documentation. We're going to set our service context. So we're going to use GPT 3.5 and I'm just going to set a global default here so I don't have to worry about passing it in.

## Building a Sub-Question Query Engine

Next step here is kind of setting up all our indexes. I could have set up a helper function for this, but I just wrote it all out. It just checks if the index actually exists in storage, and if not, it's going to create them. Right now, I do actually have them already created.

Scroll down here. So now we're going to set up our query engine, and for this particular task, you know, answering questions using multiple indexes, I'm going to use a sub-question query engine. And what this means is that basically, you'll ask a question, the LLM will look at all the indexes it has available and create sub-questions for those sub-indexes and then aggregate all the results and give a final answer. So to do this, we need a tool for each index and kind of a short little description about what that is.

Now with the Llama Index documentation, this actually makes a lot of sense because we've divided our documentation into pretty clear responsibilities, I would say. So we have kind of like a clear section for each piece of information. So we can set up those query engine tools, and then finally we can set up our sub-question query engine. Super simple. Just call `from_defaults`, give it all the tools, off we go.

## Initial Test of the Query Engine

And we could quickly test here. A quick test question: "How do I install Llama Index?" A super simple question. It should give us a reasonable answer here. Give it one second. Now, since it is calling multiple LLM calls, the response time is a bit slower. It was still not that bad. And we can see here that it correctly identified the steps to install Llama Index. So perfect. Our query engine appears to be working.

## Generating an Evaluation Question Dataset

But in order to get a fuller understanding of how it's actually working, we need to evaluate. So here I'm going to set up a sort of automated evaluation pipeline here where we're going to use GPT-4 to generate questions and then also evaluate responses.

So I'm going to generate a data set here. I'm going to load all the documentation into just like a single document object. This will make the question generation a bit more efficient because it'll be working with larger pieces of text, you know, reducing the number of LLM calls that we have to call to generate our dataset.

And so here in LlamaIndex, we have this `DataSetGenerator` object where we just give it a list of documents, in this case, our one giant document, and it will generate questions for the data that you give it. Now, I've customized the templates a little bit here to give it more context for the kinds of questions that it should answer. Now, normally you don't have to do this, it's optional, but these two here are setting up the prompt template and then also the kind of instructions that I'm giving to generate the questions. You know, I'm telling it that, you know, you're an evaluator for a search pipeline and it has to write questions using, you know, a provided documentation sample.

And here I'm telling it to generate a single question. Normally you can tell it to generate as many questions as you want, and it'll generate hopefully that number of questions per document or per node. So we call `generate_questions_from_nodes`. GPT-4 will generate those questions. This ended up generating about just over 100 questions, which was a bit too much for an evaluation pipeline, I think. So I sampled randomly 40 of them and then wrote them to disk so I don't have to call this function again. Pretty simple.

## Reviewing the Generated Questions

And down here we could take like a random sampling of five, and you can see here that these are five questions that GPT-4 had written about the documentation. And they're good questions, you know, "How can I convert tools to a LangChain tool?", "What is the function used to specify the metadata visible to the embedding model?" You know, covered that last video, very relevant. So this looks like it's working properly.

## Evaluating Response Hallucination

So now that we have our data set of questions, we have our query engine, we could just run the evaluation. So here I have set up a function, kind of a helper function to run our queries over our data. So basically what we want to do is query our query engine with our questions, keep track of all the responses, and then send those responses to the evaluator.

So here I'm kind of doing it asynchronously, but in order to avoid rate limits, I'm doing it in batches. So in this case, I'm doing it in batches of five. I get my batch of questions, I run the queries, get the responses, and then we send the responses to the evaluator. And basically, the evaluator will return yes or no. You know, yes, this response is good, or no, this response is bad. In this case, we're evaluating for hallucination in this step, so we're evaluating whether the response and the sources make sense together. You know, did the response actually come from those sources? And to do this, we're just asking GPT-4 to evaluate yes or no. And this works surprisingly well. It may sound simplistic, but it works well. It's just a little slow.

So we could get our results here. I put a little `time.sleep` at the end again to help with rate limits because we are making a lot of LLM calls here, and you don't want to get stopped in the middle of evaluation. And at the end here we return the total correct, and then just like a list of all the results, yes or no. So down here we create the response evaluator object. We make sure that we give it our GPT-4 LLM service context. We run our evaluation, and then here we print out how many of the answers were hallucinated or not. You can see at the end here, 29 out of 40 questions were answered without hallucination.

## Analyzing Hallucination Failures

That sounds not bad, but it's good to like not take this at face value and actually look at, okay, now which questions were actually, like what kind of questions were causing problems essentially? So we can use NumPy to get the, basically we can use NumPy to get the questions where the response or the result was zero, or that you know, GPT-4 was saying that the response was hallucinated. And we could see like a couple of a lot of good questions here, actually. Like, "What is the purpose of the guidance pydantic program?" "What is the purpose of the sub-question query engine?" We're using it in this notebook, that's a good question. And these are all questions that I think that the chatbot should be answering properly.

So we could kind of look at some of these questions and actually send them to the query engine and figure out why GPT-4 thinks that there's a hallucination. So we can send this first question here: "What is the response... What is the purpose of the guidance pydantic program?" and then we can get, print the response along with the sources and we'll just see what that ends up looking like. Take a second to get the response, I may as well run this other one underneath while I'm waiting. And the next question I'm going to ask is, "What is the purpose of the router query engine and how can it be used in a search pipeline?" So again, two pretty good questions, and we're going to see why GPT-4 thinks that these answers were hallucinated.

So we've got our answer here. It says, "Based on the context information, there is no specific mention of the guidance pydantic program." While that is a lie because that phrase and that class definitely appears in the documentation. We can look at the sources and we can see that it asked a question to one of the sub-indexes, "What is the purpose of the guidance pydantic program class?" and it says here the response says, "Based on the information..." So it's not finding the information. And then it also asked, "How do I install and run Llama Index?" which is, okay, not a helpful question to ask, but that's the question it asked. I'd also asked one of the basic explanations of how Llama Index works. And again, that response isn't going to really help us find the answer here. So we can kind of see that the answer here wasn't answered, but in this case, I don't know if I would call it a hallucination because it's literally repeating what this one source says. So yes and no, it's a hallucination, but it is a problematic question and that's good to know.

The second question here, "What is the purpose of the router query engine?" Router query engine in Llama Index query transformations... yeah, this is wrong. It's saying that the router query engine transforms a query into a single or multi-step process. But actually, the router query engine just takes your query and decides which sub-index to send it to. So this is completely hallucinated. And we can see here that this second, this first source here is the source of the hallucination. And then we can see on the bottom here, it did not provide any details about it. So I think the fact that the second one says that it could not find information about the router query engine is telling GPT-4 that this answer maybe is not grounded in truth. And I would agree, this is a little bit of a confusing response and it is incorrect. So again, we found two questions where our pipeline is just not working, which is great because that means we can figure out how to fix it later.

## Evaluating Answer Quality

And so this next section here is we're going to evaluate answer quality, which is a bit different than evaluating for hallucination. So in this case, we're going to look at the response and sources together and see if they have satisfied the query. And again, we're just asking an LLM that kind of question. So we're showing this to GPT-4 and it's going to return us yes or no. So again, I have a similar helper function, and again, we can set up our evaluator, except this time instead of a response evaluator, we have a query response evaluator. Pass in our GPT-4 service context, we call `evaluate`, and we can see that only 19 out of 40 questions were answered correctly.

## Analyzing Answer Quality Failures

Um, which is not great. That even if some of these are false positives, you know, that's a good indication there's a lot of room for improvement on our kind of baseline query engine. And again, we can look at which questions were answered incorrectly. Some repeats here, actually. You know, you see this guidance pydantic program question come up again and a few other ones. One that I thought was interesting was, "What is the purpose of the React agent and how can it be initialized with the other tools?" I'm kind of curious why that one wasn't answered properly. We're going to find out. And then the second one here, "What is the purpose of the load and search tool spec in the Llama Index documentation?" Again, it seems like an easy thing to answer, so it's a good thing to check in on.

Here we see that it came back with a response. The purpose of the React agent is to instantiate an agent from a set of tools. So this isn't necessarily incorrect, but I think the fact that it didn't explain how it can be initialized, like I think the fact that it didn't give an example, is telling GPT-4 that this wasn't totally satisfying the query. Which makes sense. You know, if someone asks a question like this to our documentation, our little chatbot should give an example of how to do it or otherwise it's not a really helpful response.

In this case, we have a response here, the loaded search tool spec allows users to... Yeah, this answer also sounds correct to me. So this is a case of where GPT-4 kind of falsely evaluated this. And like I said again, this process isn't perfect, but it does give us, you know, many avenues to look into for improvements and then also figure out where our query engine is going wrong. So here in this case, I think it gives a good answer. We can see that the sources look good. It did ask the same question several times, which is, I'm thinking it just didn't know which sub-index to send this question to, so it just sent it to a bunch. So that tells me this could be more efficient if our descriptions of our query tools are better represented the data that was in those tools.

## Conclusion and Next Steps

And that's pretty much it. We have our basic evaluation pipeline. We could come back to this as we develop our query pipeline further, and make improvements. And hopefully, we could come back and see that these questions that are getting answered incorrectly do get answered correctly in the future.

Alright, thanks for watching. I'll see you guys in the next one. Thanks.
